historical_claims.anchor: He died in 1940, and the work appeared posthumously in substantially censored issues of the Soviet literary magazine Moskva in 1966 and 1967.
Editions have differed as editors and scholars worked from revised typescripts and surviving manuscripts.
Bulgakov's Yeshua is not simply a transcription of the Jesus of the canonical Gospels.
Near the end Levi Matvei communicates Yeshua's request that the Master be given peace.

work.note: Existing bibliography and claim 030000-c01 identify the posthumous, censored Moskva serialization in 1966–1967. This is not the composition period or a claim that the first serialized text was unabridged.

description: Connects Moscow’s satire to the Pilate narrative, examining power, cowardice, art, love, punishment, and the survival of a manuscript. Covers Moscow's administrative imagination; Why the Roman story matters; The Master and the courage a writer might lack; Art, power, and explanation.
